title: Assessing the Implications of Inheritance Tax Reforms in the UK
gist: Oxford Economics, for Onward, models UK inheritance tax reforms: liabilities hit a record £7.0bn in 2023/24 and reach £12.6bn by 2029/30 with no change; higher nil-rate bands would cut scope sharply at a revenue cost.

insights.claim: UK inheritance tax liabilities reached a record £7.0 billion in 2023/24 and 4.7% of estates paid it, the highest share since the mid-2000s.
insights.speaker: Suki Masana
insights.so_what: Fiscal drag on frozen thresholds is a growing revenue source and political pressure point.

insights.claim: With no policy change, UK IHT liabilities are projected to reach £12.6 billion by 2029/30, with 52,100 estates liable.
insights.speaker: Suki Masana
insights.so_what: Baseline shows thresholds left frozen quietly raise revenue.

insights.claim: Raising the standard nil-rate band to £500,000 would cut 2029/30 IHT liabilities to £9.6bn and liable estates by about 40% to 31,000.
insights.speaker: Suki Masana
insights.so_what: Quantifies the revenue cost of a moderate threshold rise.

insights.claim: A £1 million standard nil-rate band would reduce liabilities to £5.8bn and liable estates to around 12,000.
insights.speaker: Suki Masana
insights.so_what: Shows the upper bound of relief and its roughly halving of revenue versus baseline.

insights.claim: Fully exempting primary residences alongside a £500,000 standard band would cut liabilities to £6.6bn and liable estates about 59% to 21,500 in 2029/30.
insights.speaker: Suki Masana
insights.so_what: Housing-wealth-heavy reforms have a large effect on scope; relevant for UK property and wealth planning.

insights.claim: Leaving IHT thresholds unchanged is itself a consequential policy decision because liabilities keep growing under current settings.
insights.speaker: Suki Masana
insights.so_what: Watch fiscal events for threshold changes; freezing is not neutral.
insights.quote: leaving thresholds unchanged is a policy decision of consequence in and of itself
